item.title: Fix: memory and Mach port leak in HP APMAgent (macOS)
item.description:
Context Link to heading

Activity Monitor showed kernel_task at ~27 GB and APMAgent at ~10 GB of reported memory, along with 219+ open Mach ports for APMAgent.

Diagnosis Link to heading

  • High kernel_task memory is normal: it’s macOS’s kernel mechanism for thermal/memory-pressure management, not a real process consuming that RAM. Not actionable.
  • APMAgent (original PID, 10+ days of uptime) actually had only ~120 MB of RSS; the inflated number in Activity Monitor comes from reported virtual/shared memory, not physical usage.
  • The real concerning data point: 219 Mach ports accumulated and 10 days 11 hours of uptime without a restart — consistent with a slow leak of internal (IPC) resources, not a network leak.
  • The process belongs to HP Insights (formerly HP TechPulse / HPDaaS), an enterprise device management agent:
    • Binary: /usr/local/share/APMAgent/APMAgent
    • LaunchDaemon: /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.hp.APMAgent.plist
    • Bundle ID: com.hp.DaasClient.macOS.APMAgent
    • Team ID: 6HB5Y2QTA3

Root causes identified in the agent’s own log Link to heading

In /var/log/APMAgent/agent.log (15 MB accumulated):

item.title: Fix: plaintext credentials in ~/.zshrc → macOS Keychain
item.description:
Context Link to heading

While reviewing brew upgrade output (keg-only PATH warnings), a full audit of ~/.zshrc turned up three plaintext credentials exported directly as environment variables:

  • GITHUB_TOKEN — GitHub personal access token
  • FIGMA_TOKEN — Figma API token
  • FULLSTORY_API_KEY — FullStory API key

Risk Link to heading

A dotfile like ~/.zshrc is sourced on every new shell, can end up in backups (Time Machine, iCloud), in a misconfigured dotfiles repo, or be read by any script/process that opens the file. Storing secrets there in plaintext means no access control at all.

item.title: Data Architecture’s Secret Weapon – RX vs. Protobuf
item.description:
In modern software development, we are often forced to choose between speed and simplicity. If you are building a system that handles massive amounts of data, you’ve likely looked at Protobuf as the standard for binary efficiency. But there is a new contender in the ring: RX (Random-Access JSON). [1, 2] While they both speak “binary,” they solve two entirely different problems. [3]

Protobuf: The Speed of Sound for APIs Link to heading

Protocol Buffers (Protobuf) are Google’s answer to slow, bloated text-based APIs. By stripping away field names and using a strict, pre-shared schema (.proto), Protobuf creates tiny payloads that fly across the network. [1, 4, 5]

item.title: `http_status` Dart Package: A Comprehensive Guide
item.description:
http_status Dart Package: A Comprehensive Guide Link to heading

Description Link to heading

  • Constants: http_status provides convenient static constants representing all HTTP status codes defined in RFC 1945 (HTTP/1.0), RFC 2616 (HTTP/1.1), and RFC 2518 (WebDAV).
  • Clarity: Each constant offers a clear name (e.g., ok, notFound, forbidden), making it easy to understand the meaning of a status code at a glance.
  • Information: Constants also provide a concise description of the status code, which can be helpful in debugging or understanding API responses.

item.title: Dart - Use late allocation if possible
item.description:
Dart v2.9 added the late modifier on variables.

When Null Safety is enabled, it is sometimes necessary to explicitly state that we will initialize a non-null variable later. Dart cannot always assume that a variable will be initialized later, as in the case of high-level variables. The following example would throw an error in Dart.

This can be used in the following two cases.

  • Late assign: promise to assign later

  • Late lazy: Initializing a variable will be later.

item.title: Fix Error 15517 MS SQL SERVER
item.description:
Fix Error 15517 MS SQL SERVER

Original link

This particular snippet of code that is used to change the owner of a database in Microsoft SQL Server, is using a system stored procedure called sp_changedbowner to perform the action.

1
2
3
4

USE [DB Name]
GO
EXEC dbo.sp_changedbowner @loginame = N'sa', @map = false
GO

Here’s the breakdown of what each line does:

  1. USE [DB Name]: This command switches the current database to the specified database. Replace [DB Name] with the name of your database.

  2. GO: In SQL Server, GO is a batch command that is used to signal the end of a batch of SQL commands. It’s not really a standard SQL command, but rather an instruction to the SQL Server client that the client should send the batch of commands to the server.

  3. EXEC dbo.sp_changedbowner @loginame = N'sa', @map = false: This command executes the stored procedure sp_changedbowner which changes the owner of the database.

    • @loginame = N'sa': This parameter specifies the login that will become the new owner of the database. In this case, it’s ‘sa’, which is the system administrator or superuser in SQL Server.

    • @map = false: This parameter determines whether objects that are still owned by the old database owner should be remapped to the new owner. If it’s set to false, no remapping will be done.

  4. GO: Again, this is the batch termination command.
